messages.subject: model does not converge due to missing factor level of endogenous variable
parts:
Hi,

I tried to fit a model to explain the presence/absence of multiple parasite species in one host species I captured in three landscapes. I am also interested in relationships between parasite species and therefore specified covariances. When I fit the model to my data the model does not converge. I removed one variable after the other and fitted each model and identified that the problem was apparently caused by the data on one specific parasite species that was only present in two out of three landscape categories  (which are predictors of the parasites presence/absence). I added an artificial data point (i.e. an infected individual) to the landscape where no infected individuals were caught and fitted the model again. This time the model converged without problems.
Is there a way to make my model converge without introducing an artificial data point? 

My code looks like this:
model11 = "#regressions
tryp.inf0 ~landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

n4.5.7~landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

n1.2 ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

n15.29 ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

picorna ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

picobirna ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

hepaci.inf ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland + sexM + Density + Chao1.10.00 + marsu

Chao1.10.00 ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland

Density ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland +Chao1.10.00

marsu ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland

#covariances
tryp.inf0 ~~ n4.5.7
tryp.inf0 ~~ n1.2
tryp.inf0 ~~ n15.29
tryp.inf0 ~~ picobirna
tryp.inf0 ~~ hepaci.inf
tryp.inf0 ~~ picorna
n4.5.7 ~~ n1.2
n4.5.7 ~~ n15.29
n4.5.7 ~~ picobirna
n4.5.7 ~~ hepaci.inf
n4.5.7 ~~ picorna
n1.2 ~~ n15.29
n1.2 ~~ picobirna
n1.2 ~~ hepaci.inf
n1.2 ~~ picorna"

model11.sem = sem(model11, data2, estimator = "WLSMV",ordered= c("tryp.inf0","n4.5.7","n1.2","n15.29","picobirna","hepaci.inf","picorna"))
summary(model11.sem, standardize = TRUE)

Thanks!
Julian

You are using the sem() function, so residual covariances between endogenous (latent response) variables will be estimated by default.  You don't need to put them into your syntax, unless you use the lavaan() function without setting auto.cov = TRUE.

the problem was apparently caused by the data on one specific parasite species that was only present in two out of three landscape categories  (which are predictors of the parasites presence/absence). I added an artificial data point (i.e. an infected individual) to the landscape where no infected individuals were caught and fitted the model again. This time the model converged without problems.
Is there a way to make my model converge without introducing an artificial data point?

Was it the reference landscape in which one of the outcomes was a constant (always 0 = absent), or was it one of the landscapes indicated by one of the 2 dummy codes?  If it was in a dummy-coded landscape, you can leave that dummy code out of the regression equation for that particular outcome (or equivalently, set that slope to zero: DV ~ 0*dummy) -- this will not affect the interpretability of the other slope.  

If it was the reference category, you could still include both dummy codes as predictors, but there is nothing for them to be "in reference" to.  With linear regression, you could identify your model by fixing the intercept to zero for that outcome, essentially turning the slopes of each dummy code into a group-specific intercept instead of a group-specific deviation from the intercept.  You could do that here to, but since it is SEM software designed with factor models in mind, the tradition has been to fix intercepts to zero anyway and estimate thresholds.  But with binary outcomes, they are equivalent: intercept = -1*threshold, so you fix either to zero to get an equivalent model.  Long story short (too late), you can fix your threshold to zero for this outcome variable to identify your model: DV | 0*th1
